chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
title: Was there a conspiracy to push the avant-garde
summary: Ridley asks about critics promoting freedom music; Sam says there were no black writers and the press called the old records alike.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Yeah. Sam, let me ask you this, to interject along the lines of this. Now being on the scene and being, you know, like one's leading jazz artist, do you feel and being involved with the business aspects, do you feel that there was any kind of conspiracy? Now I'm asking about a conspiracy from the standpoint, it seems to me like in the fifties, there were a

There are some people who feel - now I'm not asking if you agree with this or not - that there was a conspiracy that there was too much music going over there, that there were too many artists that could really play and that some people feel that it was a conspiracy with the so-called jazz critics and the writers to help push the Freedom movement, to kind of break up this heavy hold that the black artist had. Because if you notice, by pushing the avant garde all of a sudden what was going on behind the scenes in terms of the white jazz musicians, they were pushing more four-four straight ahead kind of stuff.

But this w'ole thing like with pushing these Black musicians into making this like a big thing, this was the new music, the avant garde. Do you think that there was any kind of conspiracy? I mean, because, I'm always very sensitive to like the racism that goes on. Everybody wants to talk about oh it ain't as bad as everybody wants to say, you

know but you know better than I do because you know you even experienced it even before I did, coming from down south, you know exactly what I'm talking about man. I believe that there is some kind of conspiracy. How do you feel about that? Do you feel that racism is playing a part in trying to divide and conquer the whole thing? Because that's always seem to have been a ploy that's been practiced. How do you feel about that? I mean I'm not asking you to agree with what I'm saying but I mean that seems to be a perception that a lot of people have. Do you agree with that or do you disagree with it?

Well you know any time our music gets too popular and it's going to happen again now because I see it happening now because a lot of jazz clubs is opening up and there are so many places to play. And I've seen that. But during that time there was a lot of jazz musicians on the scene but it wasn't a lot of white jazz musicians on the scene, you see. Now during that time there wasn't any black writers at all, you see. And all the writers, freaks, was white, up to the time Kenny Dorham started writing, for the DownBeat magazine. And you know how long he stayed.

You see. So I don't know if it was a conspiracy or not but they started writing oh man, we're tired of hearing this, these kind of records that all of them seem to sound the same and this and that, and this and that. So when the Freedom

come, oh this is the greatest thing I ever heard. It's different and it's more that, more vitality in it. It's got more of anything you want to call it see. Because they noticed the music was different. It was being detrimental to the guys that was doing it to themselves, you know. And so when the guy is doing this, is reading this, they get these big, like when the make these records like Ornette (Coleman)-- they get these five stars and stuff man. I'm not saying that Ornette wasn't a greater musician - I thought he was a fantastic musician when he first came from Texas.

To New York but they had so many music, man. I really fell in love with it. And through the years when they went out and started playing, they left us and left the laymen, you see. And right back to the laymen, you see.
